nameStory: Hydrilla gets its common name "waterthyme" from its superficial resemblance to the herb thyme, with small leaves arranged in whorls around the stem. The scientific name Hydrilla comes from the Greek word for water, reflecting its fully aquatic lifestyle. Unlike culinary thyme though, this plant lives entirely underwater in lakes and rivers.
description: Hydrilla is a submerged aquatic plant that forms dense underwater meadows in freshwater lakes, ponds, and rivers. Its long, branching stems can grow 3-6 feet long, creating thick mats of vegetation that can reach from the lake bottom all the way to the water surface. The plant looks like underwater greenery with small, narrow leaves arranged in circles around flexible stems. This non-native species is an aggressive grower that can quickly dominate water bodies.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves arranged in whorls of 2-8 around the stem, each about the size of a pine needle. Feel the leaf edges carefully - they have tiny serrations or spines that give them a rough texture. The midrib (center vein) often appears reddish when the plant is fresh.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, tangled underwater mats that can be several feet thick. Stems are long, flexible, and branching, growing up from the lake or river bottom toward the water surface.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, translucent flowers with red streaks and three small petals, but flowers are rarely seen since the plant reproduces mainly by breaking apart. When present, flowers float at or just below the water surface.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Long, slender, and flexible underwater stems that break easily when pulled. The broken fragments feel smooth and contain air spaces that help keep the plant buoyant.

habitat: Found in freshwater lakes, ponds, slow-moving rivers, and canals throughout New England. Prefers areas with soft sediments and can tolerate a wide range of water depths from shallow coves to deeper areas up to 20 feet. Often establishes in areas disturbed by boat traffic or where other aquatic vegetation has been removed.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from overwintering buds (turions) in the sediment as water temperatures warm. Stems begin their rapid upward growth toward the water surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when dense mats are most visible and problematic. Growth can be incredibly fast - up to an inch per day - creating thick underwater carpets.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline as water temperatures cool. Forms specialized overwintering buds that will survive in the sediment through winter.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, but hardy buds remain dormant in the lake or river bottom sediments, ready to sprout when warm weather returns.

funFact: Hydrilla can grow up to an inch per day during peak season - that's fast enough that you could literally watch it grow if you marked a stem and came back the next day!
confusionNotes: Often confused with native pondweeds and other submerged aquatics, but hydrilla's leaves in distinct whorls with serrated edges set it apart. Remember: "Hydrilla has harsh, spiny leaf edges in whorls" - the alliteration helps distinguish it from smoother-leaved native plants.
contextualKnowledge: This is an invasive species that's illegal to transport or plant in most New England states. Originally from Asia, Africa, and Australia, it was likely introduced through the aquarium trade. Despite being called "waterthyme," it's completely unrelated to the cooking herb and shouldn't be consumed.
compareHints: Hydrilla is essentially alone in its genus in New England waters, but it's often confused with native elodea (waterweed) from the same plant family. Hydrilla's leaves are arranged in more crowded whorls and have distinctly serrated edges, while elodea has smoother leaf margins and a less dense growth pattern. Hydrilla also grows much more aggressively, forming thicker mats than most native aquatic plants.
